manifest.title: Scheduling problems assembled from constraint modules

inputs.abstract:
Scheduling problems in the three-field notation $\alpha \mid \beta \mid \gamma$
are formalized as assemblies of independent fields, so that every problem is a
problem in its own right and the relations between problems follow from
relations between the values of single fields.

A kernel fixes what a schedule is. A field over a kernel is a restriction of
its instances, a constraint module that adds data and a condition on
schedules, or an objective. A specification chooses one value in every field
and determines a problem. If one specification is field by field a special
case of another, the data maps of the fields combine into an embedding of the
first problem into the second, which is sound whenever every field is. Two
families of fields cover the problems: one in which every job is a sequence of
operations, for parallel machines and shops with and without preemption, and
one for serial and parallel batching. Their fields cover machine environments,
processing times, numbers of machines and jobs, machine sets, release dates,
deadlines, precedence constraints in sixteen classes with time lags,
communication and transportation delays, a transport robot, a server with setup
times, batch setups, no-wait, no-idle, forbidden times, high multiplicity, and
sixteen objectives. Maximizing the smallest machine load and scheduling with
rejection are formalized as problems of their own.

The construction is carried out for The Scheduling Zoo. All 747 of its problems
are specifications. Three of the 614 relations in its data come from two rules
of its notation that do not hold; with the two rules corrected the data has 612
relations, and all are proved: 566 as special cases and 34 as reductions of
decision versions, each checked by evaluation, and 12 encodings that change the
instance, proved one by one. The general theorems also relate pairs of problems
of the zoo that its data does not relate.

Instances and schedules are read as words of natural numbers, every field
written through its view, the meaning its constraints use, so that the word of
an instance of a special case is also a word of its image. Against this reading,
950 results of the zoo are stated in terms of running times on the word RAM, P
and NP-hardness, fixed-parameter tractability and W[t]-hardness, as defined in
registered formalizations, and the open questions of the zoo are posed as pairs of
competing propositions. Proved transfer theorems carry results along the
relations: algorithms go down along special cases and hardness goes up, and
hardness also goes along the threshold steps between objectives, along the
encodings of machine sets, and from the standard encoding to high multiplicity.
Strong hardness, with numbers polynomial in the length of the input, is
distinguished from plain hardness throughout. Proved from the words up, building
on registered formalizations: Smith's rule decides $1 \mid\mid \sum w_jC_j$ within
$O(n \log n)$ instructions plus the length of the input;
$1 \mid r_j \mid L_{\max}$ is strongly NP-hard, and para-NP-hard in $p_{\max}$ and
in the number of distinct processing times; $P \mid M_j \mid \sum w_jZ_j$ is
fixed-parameter tractable in $m + p_{\max}$ and strongly W[1]-hard in $m$; and
$FF(1,m) \mid\mid \sum Z_j$ is strongly NP-hard and strongly W[2]-hard in $m$, while
$FF(1,m) \mid\mid \sum w_jZ_j$ is solved within $O(W n^m)$, $O(W m^{q_{\max}} n)$ and
$O(W 2^{\chi} n)$ instructions, $W$ the total weight.

concepts.title: Assembling problems from fields
concepts.description:
A family over a kernel is a collection of constraint modules and an
objective. A specification chooses one value in every field of the family. It
determines a problem: an instance is an instance of the kernel together with
admissible data for every chosen module value and for the chosen objective
value; a schedule is a schedule of the kernel; it is feasible if it
is feasible for the kernel and satisfies every module constraint; its cost is
given by the objective.

A specification $s$ is a special case of a specification $t$ if this holds
field by field; for finitely many fields this is decidable. In that case the
field-wise data maps combine into an embedding of the problem of $s$ into the
problem of $t$ that leaves the kernel instance and the schedule unchanged.

**Theorem.** If every field of the family is sound, this embedding is sound.

Consequently a relation between two problems of a family never needs a proof
of its own: it follows from the relations inside the fields.
concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Basic
import Lax434175.Problems
import Lax434175.Modules

/-!
---
title: Assembling problems from fields
type: theorem
---
A family over a kernel is a collection of constraint modules and an
objective. A specification chooses one value in every field of the family. It
determines a problem: an instance is an instance of the kernel together with
admissible data for every chosen module value and for the chosen objective
value; a schedule is a schedule of the kernel; it is feasible if it
is feasible for the kernel and satisfies every module constraint; its cost is
given by the objective.

A specification $s$ is a special case of a specification $t$ if this holds
field by field; for finitely many fields this is decidable. In that case the
field-wise data maps combine into an embedding of the problem of $s$ into the
problem of $t$ that leaves the kernel instance and the schedule unchanged.

**Theorem.** If every field of the family is sound, this embedding is sound.

Consequently a relation between two problems of a family never needs a proof
of its own: it follows from the relations inside the fields.
-/

namespace Lax434175.Assembly
open Lax434175.Problems Lax434175.Kernels Lax434175.Modules

/-- The fields from which problems over a kernel are assembled. -/
structure Family (K : Kernel) where
  /-- The names of the constraint fields. -/
  ModuleName : Type
  module : ModuleName → Module K
  objective : Objective K

/-- A choice of one value in every field. -/
structure Spec {K : Kernel} (F : Family K) where
  module : (i : F.ModuleName) → (F.module i).Value
  objective : F.objective.Value

/-- An instance of the problem described by a specification. -/
structure Inst {K : Kernel} (F : Family K) (s : Spec F) where
  base : K.Inst
  data : (i : F.ModuleName) → (F.module i).Data (s.module i) base
  admitted : ∀ i, (F.module i).admits (s.module i) base (data i)
  objectiveData : F.objective.Data s.objective base
  objectiveAdmitted : F.objective.admits s.objective base objectiveData

/-- The problem described by a specification. -/
def problem {K : Kernel} (F : Family K) (s : Spec F) : Problem where
  Inst := Inst F s
  Sched x := K.Sched x.base
  feasible x σ :=
    K.feasible x.base σ ∧ ∀ i, (F.module i).constraint (s.module i) x.base (x.data i) σ
  cost x σ := F.objective.cost s.objective x.base x.objectiveData σ

/-- Field-wise comparison of specifications. -/
def Spec.le {K : Kernel} {F : Family K} (s t : Spec F) : Prop :=
  (∀ i, (F.module i).le (s.module i) (t.module i) = true) ∧
    F.objective.le s.objective t.objective = true

instance {K : Kernel} {F : Family K} [Fintype F.ModuleName] (s t : Spec F) :
    Decidable (s.le t) := by
  unfold Spec.le
  infer_instance

/-- All fields of a family are sound. -/
structure Family.Sound {K : Kernel} (F : Family K) : Prop where
  module : ∀ i, (F.module i).Sound
  objective : F.objective.Sound

/-- The embedding induced by a field-wise comparison. The kernel instance and
the schedule are unchanged; the data of each field is read with the more
general value. -/
def lift {K : Kernel} (F : Family K) (hF : F.Sound) {s t : Spec F} (h : s.le t) :
    Embedding (problem F s) (problem F t) where
  map x :=
    { base := x.base
      data := fun i => (F.module i).embed (h.1 i) x.base (x.data i)
      admitted := fun i => (hF.module i).admits _ _ (h.1 i) x.base (x.data i) (x.admitted i)
      objectiveData := F.objective.embed h.2 x.base x.objectiveData
      objectiveAdmitted :=
        hF.objective.admits _ _ h.2 x.base x.objectiveData x.objectiveAdmitted }
  forth _ σ := σ
  back _ σ := σ

/-- The embedding induced by a field-wise comparison is sound. -/
axiom lift_sound {K : Kernel} (F : Family K) (hF : F.Sound) {s t : Spec F} (h : s.le t) :
    (lift F hF h).Sound

end Lax434175.Assembly

statements.signature:
lift_sound : ∀ {K : Lax434175.Kernels.Kernel} (F : Lax434175.Assembly.Family K) (hF : F.Sound) {s t : Lax434175.Assembly.Spec F}
  (h : s.le t), (Lax434175.Assembly.lift F hF h).Sound

concepts.title: One family for serial and parallel batching
concepts.description:
Serial and parallel batching share one machine model, in which a schedule
partitions the jobs into numbered batches and gives every batch a start time
and a processing time. All jobs of a batch start when the batch starts and
complete when it completes, at its start plus its processing time. A
schedule is feasible for this model if a setup precedes every batch, as in
batch scheduling.

The batching field has the values serial and parallel: the processing time of
every batch is the sum, or the maximum, of the processing times of its jobs.
The two values are incomparable. The other fields are those of batching.

A batching problem in a mode determines the problem of this family with the
same values and that mode.

**Theorem.** The two problems are special cases of each other. The fields of
the family are sound, so that a specification that is field by field a
special case of another describes a special case of the other's problem, and
one that reduces to another describes a problem whose decision version
reduces to that of the other.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax434175.BatchProblems

/-!
---
title: One family for serial and parallel batching
type: theorem
---
Serial and parallel batching share one machine model, in which a schedule
partitions the jobs into numbered batches and gives every batch a start time
and a processing time. All jobs of a batch start when the batch starts and
complete when it completes, at its start plus its processing time. A
schedule is feasible for this model if a setup precedes every batch, as in
batch scheduling.

The batching field has the values serial and parallel: the processing time of
every batch is the sum, or the maximum, of the processing times of its jobs.
The two values are incomparable. The other fields are those of batching.

A batching problem in a mode determines the problem of this family with the
same values and that mode.

**Theorem.** The two problems are special cases of each other. The fields of
the family are sound, so that a specification that is field by field a
special case of another describes a special case of the other's problem, and
one that reduces to another describes a problem whose decision version
reduces to that of the other.
-/

namespace Lax434175.BatchFamily
open Lax434175.Problems Lax434175.Kernels Lax434175.Modules Lax434175.Assembly
open Lax434175
open Lax434175.Batching (Inst Capacity ProcessingTimes members)

/-- A batch schedule with the processing time of every batch. -/
structure Sched (x : Inst) where
  /-- The number of the batch of a job. -/
  batch : Fin x.jobs → ℕ
  /-- The start time of a batch. -/
  start : ℕ → ℕ
  /-- The processing time of a batch. -/
  length : ℕ → ℕ

/-- The batches and start times of a schedule. -/
def Sched.plain {x : Inst} (σ : Sched x) : Batching.Sched x := ⟨σ.batch, σ.start⟩

/-- The completion time of a batch. -/
def finish {x : Inst} (σ : Sched x) (k : ℕ) : ℕ := σ.start k + σ.length k

/-- A setup precedes every batch. -/
def feasible (x : Inst) (σ : Sched x) : Prop :=
  (∀ j, x.setup ≤ σ.start (σ.batch j)) ∧
  ∀ i j, σ.batch i < σ.batch j → finish σ (σ.batch i) + x.setup ≤ σ.start (σ.batch j)

/-- The kernel of batch scheduling. -/
def kernel : Kernel where
  Inst := Inst
  jobs := Inst.jobs
  release := Inst.r
  Sched := Sched
  feasible := feasible
  start _ σ j := (σ.start (σ.batch j) : NNRat)
  completion _ σ j := (finish σ (σ.batch j) : NNRat)

def modeLe : Batching.Mode → Batching.Mode → Bool
  | .serial, .serial | .parallel, .parallel => true
  | _, _ => false

/-- The batching field. -/
def mode : Module kernel where
  Value := Batching.Mode
  Data _ _ := Unit
  admits _ _ _ := True
  constraint v x _ σ := ∀ k, σ.length k = Batching.length v x σ.plain k
  le := modeLe
  embed _ _ _ := ()

/-- The capacity field. -/
def capacity : Module kernel where
  Value := Capacity
  Data := Capacity.Data
  admits _ _ _ := True
  constraint v _ d σ := ∀ k, ∑ j ∈ members σ.plain k, v.size d j ≤ v.bound d
  le := Capacity.le
  embed := Capacity.embed

/-- The processing-time field. -/
def processingTimes : Module kernel :=
  Module.ofRestriction ProcessingTimes ProcessingTimes.holds
    (fun v w => decide (v.rank ≤ w.rank))

/-- The fields of the family: batching and the fields of batch scheduling. -/
inductive FieldName
  | mode
  | field (i : BatchProblems.FieldName)
  deriving DecidableEq

instance : Fintype FieldName where
  elems := {.mode, .field .capacity, .field .jobCount, .field .processingTimes,
    .field .releaseDates, .field .deadlines, .field .precedence}
  complete x := by
    cases x with
    | mode => decide
    | field i => cases i <;> decide

/-- The batching problems. -/
abbrev family : Family kernel :=
  Thresholds.family FieldName fun
    | .mode => mode
    | .field .capacity => capacity
    | .field .jobCount => Counts.module _ kernel.jobs
    | .field .processingTimes => processingTimes
    | .field .releaseDates => ReleaseDates.module _
    | .field .deadlines => Deadlines.module _
    | .field .precedence => Precedence.oneMachine _

instance : Fintype family.ModuleName :=
  inferInstanceAs (Fintype FieldName)

/-- The specification `1 | β | γ` of a batching problem. -/
def spec (mode : Batching.Mode) (capacity : Capacity)
    (jobCount : Counts.Bound := .any)
    (processingTimes : ProcessingTimes := .arbitrary)
    (release : ReleaseDates.Value := .none)
    (deadline : Deadlines.Value := .none)
    (precedence : Precedence.Value := .none)
    (objective : Objectives.Value) : Spec family where
  module
    | .mode => mode
    | .field .capacity => capacity
    | .field .jobCount => jobCount
    | .field .processingTimes => processingTimes
    | .field .releaseDates => release
    | .field .deadlines => deadline
    | .field .precedence => precedence
  objective := objective

/-- The specification of the family with the values of a batching problem in
a mode. -/
def ofSpec (m : Batching.Mode) (s : Spec (BatchProblems.family m)) : Spec family where
  module
    | .mode => m
    | .field .capacity => s.module .capacity
    | .field .jobCount => s.module .jobCount
    | .field .processingTimes => s.module .processingTimes
    | .field .releaseDates => s.module .releaseDates
    | .field .deadlines => s.module .deadlines
    | .field .precedence => s.module .precedence
  objective := s.objective

axiom faithful (m : Batching.Mode) (s : Spec (BatchProblems.family m)) :
    SpecialCase (problem _ s) (problem family (ofSpec m s)) ∧
      SpecialCase (problem family (ofSpec m s)) (problem _ s)

axiom family_sound : family.Sound

axiom specialCase_of_le {s t : Spec family} :
    s.le t → SpecialCase (problem family s) (problem family t)

axiom reducible_of_reduces {s t : Spec family} :
    Thresholds.Reduces s t → Reducible (problem family s) (problem family t)

end Lax434175.BatchFamily

statements.signature:
faithful : ∀ (m : Lax434175.Batching.Mode) (s : Lax434175.Assembly.Spec (Lax434175.BatchProblems.family m)),
  And
    (Lax434175.Problems.SpecialCase (Lax434175.Assembly.problem (Lax434175.BatchProblems.family m) s)
      (Lax434175.Assembly.problem Lax434175.BatchFamily.family (Lax434175.BatchFamily.ofSpec m s)))
    (Lax434175.Problems.SpecialCase
      (Lax434175.Assembly.problem Lax434175.BatchFamily.family (Lax434175.BatchFamily.ofSpec m s))
      (Lax434175.Assembly.problem (Lax434175.BatchProblems.family m) s))
family_sound : Lax434175.BatchFamily.family.Sound

reducible_of_reduces : ∀ {s t : Lax434175.Assembly.Spec Lax434175.BatchFamily.family},
  Lax434175.Thresholds.Reduces s t →
    Lax434175.Problems.Reducible (Lax434175.Assembly.problem Lax434175.BatchFamily.family s)
      (Lax434175.Assembly.problem Lax434175.BatchFamily.family t)

specialCase_of_le : ∀ {s t : Lax434175.Assembly.Spec Lax434175.BatchFamily.family},
  s.le t →
    Lax434175.Problems.SpecialCase (Lax434175.Assembly.problem Lax434175.BatchFamily.family s)
      (Lax434175.Assembly.problem Lax434175.BatchFamily.family t)

concepts.title: Batch scheduling on a single machine
concepts.description:
An instance has $n$ jobs with processing times $p_j$ and a setup time $s$. A
schedule partitions the jobs into batches, numbered in the order in which
they are processed, and assigns a start time to every batch. All jobs of a
batch start when the batch starts and complete when the batch completes.

There are two modes. In serial batching the processing time of a batch is
the sum of the processing times of its jobs; in parallel batching it is
their maximum.

A schedule is feasible for the kernel if a setup precedes every batch: a
batch starts no earlier than time $s$, and no earlier than $s$ time units
after the completion of every batch with a smaller number.

The capacity field has the values

- unbounded: a batch may contain any number of jobs;
- bounded: a number $b$ is given, and a batch contains at most $b$ jobs;
- sizes: a number $b$ and a size for every job are given, and the sizes of
  the jobs of a batch sum to at most $b$.

Unbounded is the special case $b = n$ of bounded, and bounded the special
case of sizes in which every job has size $1$.

The processing-time field restricts the instances to unit or to equal
processing times.

**Theorem.** In both modes the capacity field and the processing-time field
are sound.
concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib.Algebra.BigOperators.Group.Finset.Basic
import Mathlib.Data.Finset.Lattice.Fold
import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.BigOperators
import Mathlib.Data.NNRat.Defs
import Lax434175.Modules

/-!
---
title: Batch scheduling on a single machine
type: theorem
---
An instance has $n$ jobs with processing times $p_j$ and a setup time $s$. A
schedule partitions the jobs into batches, numbered in the order in which
they are processed, and assigns a start time to every batch. All jobs of a
batch start when the batch starts and complete when the batch completes.

There are two modes. In serial batching the processing time of a batch is
the sum of the processing times of its jobs; in parallel batching it is
their maximum.

A schedule is feasible for the kernel if a setup precedes every batch: a
batch starts no earlier than time $s$, and no earlier than $s$ time units
after the completion of every batch with a smaller number.

The capacity field has the values

- unbounded: a batch may contain any number of jobs;
- bounded: a number $b$ is given, and a batch contains at most $b$ jobs;
- sizes: a number $b$ and a size for every job are given, and the sizes of
  the jobs of a batch sum to at most $b$.

Unbounded is the special case $b = n$ of bounded, and bounded the special
case of sizes in which every job has size $1$.

The processing-time field restricts the instances to unit or to equal
processing times.

**Theorem.** In both modes the capacity field and the processing-time field
are sound.
-/

namespace Lax434175.Batching
open Lax434175.Kernels Lax434175.Modules

structure Inst where
  jobs : ℕ
  p : Fin jobs → ℕ
  /-- The release date of a job. -/
  r : Fin jobs → ℕ
  /-- The setup time before every batch. -/
  setup : ℕ

inductive Mode
  | serial
  | parallel

structure Sched (x : Inst) where
  /-- The number of the batch of a job. -/
  batch : Fin x.jobs → ℕ
  /-- The start time of a batch. -/
  start : ℕ → ℕ

/-- The jobs of a batch. -/
def members {x : Inst} (σ : Sched x) (k : ℕ) : Finset (Fin x.jobs) :=
  Finset.univ.filter (fun j => σ.batch j = k)

/-- The processing time of a batch. -/
def length (mode : Mode) (x : Inst) (σ : Sched x) (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  match mode with
  | .serial => ∑ j ∈ members σ k, x.p j
  | .parallel => (members σ k).sup x.p

/-- The completion time of a batch. -/
def finish (mode : Mode) (x : Inst) (σ : Sched x) (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  σ.start k + length mode x σ k

/-- A setup precedes every batch. -/
def feasible (mode : Mode) (x : Inst) (σ : Sched x) : Prop :=
  (∀ j, x.setup ≤ σ.start (σ.batch j)) ∧
  ∀ i j, σ.batch i < σ.batch j →
    finish mode x σ (σ.batch i) + x.setup ≤ σ.start (σ.batch j)

/-- The kernel of batch scheduling in a mode. -/
def kernel (mode : Mode) : Kernel where
  Inst := Inst
  jobs := Inst.jobs
  release := Inst.r
  Sched := Sched
  feasible := feasible mode
  start _ σ j := (σ.start (σ.batch j) : NNRat)
  completion x σ j := (finish mode x σ (σ.batch j) : NNRat)

inductive Capacity
  | unbounded
  | bounded
  | sizes

/-- The data of a capacity value. -/
def Capacity.Data : Capacity → Inst → Type
  | .unbounded, _ => Unit
  | .bounded, _ => ℕ
  | .sizes, x => ℕ × (Fin x.jobs → ℕ)

/-- The capacity of a batch; the number of jobs when unbounded. -/
def Capacity.bound {x : Inst} : (v : Capacity) → v.Data x → ℕ
  | .unbounded, _ => x.jobs
  | .bounded, b => b
  | .sizes, d => d.1

/-- The size of a job; `1` without sizes. -/
def Capacity.size {x : Inst} : (v : Capacity) → v.Data x → Fin x.jobs → ℕ
  | .unbounded, _ => fun _ => 1
  | .bounded, _ => fun _ => 1
  | .sizes, d => d.2

def Capacity.le : Capacity → Capacity → Bool
  | .unbounded, _ => true
  | .bounded, .unbounded => false
  | .bounded, _ => true
  | .sizes, .sizes => true
  | .sizes, _ => false

def Capacity.embed : {v w : Capacity} → Capacity.le v w = true → (x : Inst) →
    v.Data x → w.Data x
  | _, .unbounded, _, _, _ => ()
  | v, .bounded, _, _, d => v.bound d
  | v, .sizes, _, _, d => (v.bound d, v.size d)

/-- The capacity field. -/
def capacity (mode : Mode) : Module (kernel mode) where
  Value := Capacity
  Data := Capacity.Data
  admits _ _ _ := True
  constraint v _ d σ := ∀ k, ∑ j ∈ members σ k, v.size d j ≤ v.bound d
  le := Capacity.le
  embed := Capacity.embed

inductive ProcessingTimes
  | unit
  | equal
  | arbitrary

/-- The instances of a processing-time restriction. -/
def ProcessingTimes.holds : ProcessingTimes → Inst → Prop
  | .unit, x => ∀ j, x.p j = 1
  | .equal, x => ∃ p, ∀ j, x.p j = p
  | .arbitrary, _ => True

/-- The position of a value in the chain unit, equal, arbitrary. -/
def ProcessingTimes.rank : ProcessingTimes → ℕ
  | .unit => 0
  | .equal => 1
  | .arbitrary => 2

/-- The processing-time field. -/
def processingTimes (mode : Mode) : Module (kernel mode) :=
  Module.ofRestriction ProcessingTimes ProcessingTimes.holds
    (fun v w => decide (v.rank ≤ w.rank))

axiom capacity_sound (mode : Mode) : (capacity mode).Sound

axiom processingTimes_sound (mode : Mode) : (processingTimes mode).Sound

end Lax434175.Batching

statements.signature: capacity_sound : ∀ (mode : Lax434175.Batching.Mode), (Lax434175.Batching.capacity mode).Sound
processingTimes_sound : ∀ (mode : Lax434175.Batching.Mode), (Lax434175.Batching.processingTimes mode).Sound

concepts.title: Scheduling on one machine as batching
concepts.description:
Batching with setup time $0$ and batches of at most one job is scheduling on a
single machine: the batches are processed one after the other, and a batch
with one job takes the processing time of that job, in serial and in parallel
batching alike. Conversely, numbering the jobs of a non-preemptive schedule on
one machine by start time (ties by completion time and then by number) and
putting each job in a batch of its own gives such a batch schedule with the
same start and completion times.

In serial batching the capacity may also be unbounded. With setup time $0$,
splitting a batch into its jobs, processed one after the other in the order of
their numbers from the start of the batch, completes no job later and starts
none earlier than the batch. For a regular objective, one that does not
decrease when a completion time grows (every objective here except the
just-in-time ones), a batch schedule therefore gives a schedule on one
machine of no larger cost.

Hence a problem of the family with operations that has one operation per job,
one machine, no interruption, no machine-set restriction, processing times
unit, equal or arbitrary, a precedence class other than $A_m$-orders, and
none of the server, forbidden times, no-idle constraints and batch setups,
reduces to the batching problem with the same number of jobs, processing
times, release dates, deadlines, precedence constraints and objective: with
bounded capacity, in either mode, and with unbounded capacity in serial mode
when the objective is regular.

A specification $s$ of the family with operations reduces to a specification
$t$ of the batching family if $s$ is of this kind and the batching
specification obtained from it, in a mode and a capacity allowed for it, is
field by field a special case of $t$.

**Theorem.** A specification that reduces to a batching specification
describes a problem whose decision version reduces to that of the batching
problem.

/-!

title: Scheduling on one machine as batching
type: theorem
---
Batching with setup time $0$ and batches of at most one job is scheduling on a
single machine: the batches are processed one after the other, and a batch
with one job takes the processing time of that job, in serial and in parallel
batching alike. Conversely, numbering the jobs of a non-preemptive schedule on
one machine by start time (ties by completion time and then by number) and
putting each job in a batch of its own gives such a batch schedule with the
same start and completion times.

their numbers from the start of the batch, completes no job later and starts
none earlier than the batch. For a regular objective, one that does not
decrease when a completion time grows (every objective here except the
just-in-time ones), a batch schedule therefore gives a schedule on one
machine of no larger cost.

Hence a problem of the family with operations that has one operation per job,
one machine, no interruption, no machine-set restriction, processing times
unit, equal or arbitrary, a precedence class other than $A_m$-orders, and
none of the server, forbidden times, no-idle constraints and batch setups,
reduces to the batching problem with the same number of jobs, processing
times, release dates, deadlines, precedence constraints and objective: with
bounded capacity, in either mode, and with unbounded capacity in serial mode
when the objective is regular.

A specification $s$ of the family with operations reduces to a specification
$t$ of the batching family if $s$ is of this kind and the batching
specification obtained from it, in a mode and a capacity allowed for it, is
field by field a special case of $t$.

**Theorem.** A specification that reduces to a batching specification
describes a problem whose decision version reduces to that of the batching
problem.
-/

namespace Lax434175.BatchingZeroSetup
open Lax434175.Problems Lax434175.Assembly
open Lax434175 Lax434175.Operations Lax434175.OperationsFamily Lax434175.TimeReversal
open Lax434175.PreemptionUseless

def isNoneMode : Interruption.Mode → Bool
  | .none => true
  | _ => false

def noSets : Machines → Bool
  | .par .none => true
  | _ => false

def notAOrder : Precedence.Order → Bool
  | .aOrder => false
  | _ => true

/-- The processing-time value of batching with the same instances. -/
def batchTimes : ParallelMachines.ProcessingTimes → Option Batching.ProcessingTimes
  | .unit => some .unit
  | .equal => some .equal
  | .arbitrary => some .arbitrary
  | .oneOrTwo => none

/-- The specification is a single-machine problem that batching expresses. -/
def Applies (s : Spec family) : Bool :=
  isNoneMode (s.module .interruption) && isSingle (s.module .jobStructure) &&
    atMostOne (s.module .machineCount) && (batchTimes (s.module .processingTimes)).isSome &&
    noSets (s.module .machineSets) && notAOrder (s.module .precedence).order &&
    noServer (s.module .server) && noForbidden (s.module .forbiddenTimes) &&
    noIdling (s.module .noIdle) && noSetups (s.module .batchSetups)

/-- The objective does not decrease when a completion time grows: every
objective except the just-in-time ones. -/
def isRegular (o : Objectives.Value) : Bool :=
  Objectives.kind o != .notJustInTime

/-- The capacities a single-machine problem is read in: at most one job per
batch in either mode, and unbounded capacity in serial mode for a regular
objective. -/
def capacityAllowed : Batching.Mode → Batching.Capacity → Objectives.Value → Bool
  | _, .bounded, _ => true
  | .serial, .unbounded, o => isRegular o
  | _, _, _ => false

/-- The batching specification of a single-machine specification. -/
def toBatch (s : Spec family) (mode : Batching.Mode) (times : Batching.ProcessingTimes)
    (capacity : Batching.Capacity) : Spec BatchFamily.family where
  module
    | .mode => mode
    | .field .capacity => capacity
    | .field .jobCount => s.module .jobCount
    | .field .processingTimes => times
    | .field .releaseDates => s.module .releaseDates
    | .field .deadlines => s.module .deadlines
    | .field .precedence => s.module .precedence
  objective := s.objective

/-- `s` reduces to the batching specification `t`. -/
def ReducesToBatching (s : Spec family) (t : Spec BatchFamily.family) : Prop :=
  Applies s = true ∧ ∃ mode times capacity, batchTimes (s.module .processingTimes) = some times ∧
    capacityAllowed mode capacity s.objective = true ∧ (toBatch s mode times capacity).le t

instance (s : Spec family) (t : Spec BatchFamily.family) : Decidable (ReducesToBatching s t) := by
  unfold ReducesToBatching
  cases h : batchTimes (s.module .processingTimes) with
  | none => exact isFalse fun ⟨_, _, _, _, hm, _⟩ => by simp at hm
  | some w =>
    exact decidable_of_iff (Applies s = true ∧
      ∃ mode ∈ [Batching.Mode.serial, .parallel],
        ∃ capacity ∈ [Batching.Capacity.unbounded, .bounded, .sizes],
          capacityAllowed mode capacity s.objective = true ∧ (toBatch s mode w capacity).le t)
      ⟨fun ⟨h1, mode, _, capacity, _, h2, h3⟩ => ⟨h1, mode, w, capacity, rfl, h2, h3⟩,
       fun ⟨h1, mode, w', capacity, hw, h2, h3⟩ => by
        cases hw
        refine ⟨h1, mode, ?_, capacity, ?_, h2, h3⟩
        · cases mode <;> simp
        · cases capacity <;> simp⟩

axiom reducible_of_reducesToBatching {s : Spec family} {t : Spec BatchFamily.family} :
    ReducesToBatching s t → Reducible (problem family s) (problem BatchFamily.family t)

end Lax434175.BatchingZeroSetup

import Lax434175.Assembly
import Lax434175.Counts
import Lax434175.ReleaseDates
import Lax434175.Deadlines
import Lax434175.Precedence
import Lax434175.Thresholds
import Lax434175.Batching

/-!
---
title: Batching problems in three-field notation
type: theorem
---
The family of batching problems in a mode has the constraint fields
capacity, number of jobs, processing times, release dates, deadlines and
precedence constraints, and the completion-time objectives.

A problem $1 \mid \beta \mid \gamma$ whose $\beta$ contains s-batch or
p-batch is one specification of the family of serial or of parallel
batching. For example $1 \mid \text{p-batch}(\infty) \mid \sum w_j C_j$ and
$1 \mid \text{p-batch}, r_j \mid \sum w_j T_j$ are the specifications below.
The concept on one family for batching joins the two modes into a single
family with a batching field.

**Theorem.** In both modes, a specification that reduces to another
describes a problem whose decision version reduces to that of the other; if
it is field by field a special case, it describes a special case.
-/

namespace Lax434175.BatchProblems
open Lax434175.Problems Lax434175.Kernels Lax434175.Modules Lax434175.Assembly
open Lax434175

/-- The constraint fields of the family. -/
inductive FieldName
  | capacity
  | jobCount
  | processingTimes
  | releaseDates
  | deadlines
  | precedence
  deriving DecidableEq

instance : Fintype FieldName where
  elems := {.capacity, .jobCount, .processingTimes, .releaseDates, .deadlines, .precedence}
  complete x := by cases x <;> decide

/-- The batching problems of a mode. -/
abbrev family (mode : Batching.Mode) : Family (Batching.kernel mode) :=
  Thresholds.family FieldName fun
    | .capacity => Batching.capacity mode
    | .jobCount => Counts.module _ (Batching.kernel mode).jobs
    | .processingTimes => Batching.processingTimes mode
    | .releaseDates => ReleaseDates.module _
    | .deadlines => Deadlines.module _
    | .precedence => Precedence.oneMachine _

/-- The specification `1 | β | γ` of a batching problem. -/
def spec (mode : Batching.Mode) (capacity : Batching.Capacity)
    (jobCount : Counts.Bound := .any)
    (processingTimes : Batching.ProcessingTimes := .arbitrary)
    (release : ReleaseDates.Value := .none)
    (deadline : Deadlines.Value := .none)
    (precedence : Precedence.Value := .none)
    (objective : Objectives.Value) : Spec (family mode) where
  module
    | .capacity => capacity
    | .jobCount => jobCount
    | .processingTimes => processingTimes
    | .releaseDates => release
    | .deadlines => deadline
    | .precedence => precedence
  objective := objective

/-- `1 | p-batch(∞) | Σw_jC_j` -/
def parallel_unbounded_sumWC : Spec (family .parallel) :=
  spec _ (capacity := .unbounded) (objective := .sumWC)

/-- `1 | p-batch, r_j | Σw_jT_j` -/
def parallel_bounded_release_sumWT : Spec (family .parallel) :=
  spec _ (capacity := .bounded) (release := .releaseDates) (objective := .sumWT)

axiom family_sound (mode : Batching.Mode) : (family mode).Sound

axiom specialCase_of_le (mode : Batching.Mode) {s t : Spec (family mode)} :
    s.le t → SpecialCase (problem (family mode) s) (problem (family mode) t)

axiom reducible_of_reduces (mode : Batching.Mode) {s t : Spec (family mode)} :
    Thresholds.Reduces s t → Reducible (problem (family mode) s) (problem (family mode) t)

end Lax434175.BatchProblems

concepts.title: Problems with bounds on parameters
concepts.description:
Some special cases of a problem are not a choice of one value per field: they
bound a quantity that reads several fields at once. Zero slack, $d_j = r_j + p_j$,
reads the release date (kernel), the processing time (kernel) and the due date
(objective), so no single field can express it. Such a special case is a
*bounded problem*: the instances of a problem on which finitely many parameters
are at most given numbers. A parameter is any function of the instance into the
naturals, so "slack at most $\sigma$", "window at most $k$" and
"$p_{\max} \le k$" are all bounds.

A bounded problem is a restriction of its problem, so it is a special case of
it by the inclusion of instances, and a reading of the problem is a reading of
the bounded problem on the same words.

**Theorem.** A bounded problem is a special case of its problem.

**Theorem.** A sound embedding of $A$ in $B$ that maps every instance within the
bounds of $A$ to an instance within the bounds of $B$ makes the bounded problem
of $A$ a special case of the bounded problem of $B$. If it maps every instance
of $A$ within the bounds of $B$, then $A$ itself is a special case of the
bounded problem of $B$.

On one machine with release dates and due dates, the *due-date slack* of a job
is $d_j - r_j - p_j$, truncated at $0$, and the parameter is its largest value
over the jobs. Bounding it by $0$ gives the problem in which no job has room to
move: $d_j \le r_j + p_j$ for every job, so a job is on time exactly when it
starts at its release date and completes at its due date $d_j = r_j + p_j$, or it
cannot be on time at all.

**Theorem.** $1 \mid\mid \sum w_j Z_j$ is a special case of
$1 \mid r_j \mid \sum w_j U_j$ with due-date slack $0$: the encoding with release
dates $r_j = d_j - p_j$ produces only instances of slack $0$.

namespace Lax434175.Bounded
open Lax434175 Lax434175.Problems Lax434175.Parameters Lax434175.Assembly
open Lax434175.ParallelMachines Lax434175.ParallelProblems Lax434175.Encodings

/-- A bound `κ ≤ k` on a parameter of a problem. -/
structure Bound (P : Problem) where
  /-- The parameter. -/
  param : Parameter P
  /-- Its largest admitted value. -/
  value : ℕ

/-- The instance is within every bound of the list. -/
def holds {P : Problem} (bs : List (Bound P)) (x : P.Inst) : Prop :=
  ∀ b ∈ bs, b.param x ≤ b.value

/-- The bounded problem: the instances of `P` within the bounds `bs`. -/
def bounded (P : Problem) (bs : List (Bound P)) : Problem :=
  P.restrict (holds bs)

/-- A reading of a problem read on the instances of a bounded problem: the same
words. -/
def reading {P : Problem} (R : Results.PReading P) (bs : List (Bound P)) :
    Results.PReading (bounded P bs) where
  Encodes w x := R.Encodes w x.1
  Decodes x w σ := R.Decodes x.1 w σ
  reveal := ⟨fun x y t => R.reveal.same x.1 y.1 t, fun x y σ τ t => R.reveal.agree x.1 y.1 σ τ t⟩

axiom bounded_specialCase (P : Problem) (bs : List (Bound P)) : SpecialCase (bounded P bs) P

axiom bounded_mono {A B : Problem} (e : Embedding A B) (he : e.Sound)
    (bs : List (Bound A)) (cs : List (Bound B)) (h : ∀ x, holds bs x → holds cs (e.map x)) :
    SpecialCase (bounded A bs) (bounded B cs)

axiom specialCase_bounded {A B : Problem} (e : Embedding A B) (he : e.Sound)
    (cs : List (Bound B)) (h : ∀ x, holds cs (e.map x)) : SpecialCase A (bounded B cs)

/-- The largest due-date slack `d_j - r_j - p_j`, truncated at `0`, on parallel
machines; `p_j` is the time of the job on all its machines together, which on
one machine is its processing time. A due date is `0` when the objective has
none. -/
def dueSlack (s : Spec nonpreemptive) : Parameter (problem nonpreemptive s) := fun x =>
  Finset.univ.sup fun j =>
    Objectives.dueDate (K := Nonpreemptive.model.kernel) s.objective x.objectiveData j
      - x.base.r j - duration x.base j Finset.univ

/-- `1 | r_j, d_j ≤ r_j + p_j | Σ w_j U_j`: one machine, release dates, weighted
late jobs, and due-date slack `0`. -/
def zeroSlackWeightedLate : Problem :=
  bounded (problem nonpreemptive (singleRelease .sumWU)) [⟨dueSlack (singleRelease .sumWU), 0⟩]

axiom weightedJustInTime_zeroSlack :
    SpecialCase (problem nonpreemptive (single .sumWZ)) zeroSlackWeightedLate

end Lax434175.Bounded

      (∀ (x : A.Inst), Lax434175.Bounded.holds bs x → Lax434175.Bounded.holds cs (e.map x)) →
        Lax434175.Problems.SpecialCase (Lax434175.Bounded.bounded A bs) (Lax434175.Bounded.bounded B cs)

concepts.title: Communication delays
concepts.description:
The communication-delay field of a machine model on parallel machines has
the values

- none: no delays;
- unit: a set of ordered pairs of jobs is given; if $(i, j)$ is such a pair
  and the two jobs are processed on different sets of machines, then job $j$
  may not start before one time unit after the completion of job $i$;
- general: for some ordered pairs of jobs a delay $c_{ij}$ is given, and the
  same holds with $c_{ij}$ in place of one time unit.

The pairs with a delay are those related by the precedence constraints of
the problem; the delay adds to the precedence constraint only when the two
jobs are not processed in the same place.

No delays is the special case without pairs; unit delays are the special
case $c_{ij} = 1$.

**Theorem.** Over every machine model, the communication-delay field is
sound.

import Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Field.Rat
import Lax434175.ParallelMachines

/-!
---
title: Communication delays
type: theorem
---
The communication-delay field of a machine model on parallel machines has
the values

- none: no delays;
- unit: a set of ordered pairs of jobs is given; if $(i, j)$ is such a pair
  and the two jobs are processed on different sets of machines, then job $j$
  may not start before one time unit after the completion of job $i$;
- general: for some ordered pairs of jobs a delay $c_{ij}$ is given, and the
  same holds with $c_{ij}$ in place of one time unit.

The pairs with a delay are those related by the precedence constraints of
the problem; the delay adds to the precedence constraint only when the two
jobs are not processed in the same place.

No delays is the special case without pairs; unit delays are the special
case $c_{ij} = 1$.

**Theorem.** Over every machine model, the communication-delay field is
sound.
-/

namespace Lax434175.CommunicationDelays
open Lax434175.Kernels Lax434175.Modules Lax434175.ParallelMachines

inductive Value
  | none
  | unit
  | general

/-- The data of a value. -/
def Data : Value → Inst → Type
  | .none, _ => Unit
  | .unit, x => Fin x.jobs → Fin x.jobs → Prop
  | .general, x => Fin x.jobs → Fin x.jobs → ℕ → Prop

/-- `view v d i j c`: the pair `(i, j)` has the delay `c`. -/
def view {x : Inst} : (v : Value) → Data v x → Fin x.jobs → Fin x.jobs → ℕ → Prop
  | .none, _ => fun _ _ _ => False
  | .unit, r => fun i j c => r i j ∧ c = 1
  | .general, d => d

def le : Value → Value → Bool
  | .none, _ => true
  | .unit, .none => false
  | .unit, _ => true
  | .general, .general => true
  | .general, _ => false

def embed : {v w : Value} → le v w = true → (x : Inst) → Data v x → Data w x
  | _, .none, _, _, _ => ()
  | .none, .unit, _, _, _ => fun _ _ => False
  | .unit, .unit, _, _, d => d
  | v, .general, _, _, d => view v d
  | .general, .unit, h, _, _ => absurd h Bool.false_ne_true

/-- The communication-delay field of a machine model. -/
def module (M : Model) : Module M.kernel where
  Value := Value
  Data v x := Data v (M.inst x)
  admits _ _ _ := True
  constraint v x d σ := ∀ i j c, view v d i j c → ∀ S S', M.uses x σ i S → M.uses x σ j S' →
    S ≠ S' →
    (M.kernel.completion x σ (Fin.cast (M.jobs_eq x).symm i) : ℚ) + (c : ℚ) ≤
      (M.kernel.start x σ (Fin.cast (M.jobs_eq x).symm j) : ℚ)
  le := le
  embed h x d := embed h (M.inst x) d

axiom sound (M : Model) : (module M).Sound

end Lax434175.CommunicationDelays

concepts.title: Complexity classes along special cases
concepts.description:
The classes are those of the word RAM, for parameterized problems on words: a
set of admissible words, the yes-instances among them, and a parameter.

- **P**: one program decides the problem in polynomial time on its
  admissible words.
- **NP-hard**: every language in NP, written as words of zeros and ones,
  reduces to the problem in polynomial time on admissible words.
- **FPT**, **W[t]** and hardness for a class are those of the registered
  W-hierarchy (lax-496464).
- **XP**: one program decides the problem within $(|x|+2)^{f(k)}$
  instructions for a computable $f$, where $|x|$ is the bit size of the word
  and $k$ its parameter.
- **para-NP-hard**: the problem restricted to the words of parameter at most
  some $k$ is NP-hard.

A problem $A$ refines a problem $B$ if every admissible word of $A$ is one of
$B$, with the same answer and the same parameter.

**Theorem.** If $A$ refines $B$, then $B$ in P, FPT or XP puts $A$ there,
and $A$ NP-hard, para-NP-hard or hard for a class of parameterized problems
makes $B$ so.

**Theorem.** For a coding of a family of scheduling problems with sound
fields, the problem of a field-wise special case $s$ of $t$ refines that of
$t$, for every parameter of the kernel instance and every invariant parameter
of a constraint field.

namespace Lax434175.ComplexityClasses
open Lax434175.Kernels Lax434175.Modules Lax434175.Assembly
open Lax434175.Parameters Lax434175.WordProblems
open Lax808846.Ram Lax759944.BinaryWordEncoding Lax759944.RamPolytime

open Lax888481.ParameterizedComplexity (Problem)

/-- The answer a deciding program writes. -/
noncomputable def answer (P : Problem) (x : List ℕ) : List ℕ :=
  open Classical in if P.Yes x then [1] else [0]

/-- `P` is in **P**. -/
def InP (P : Problem) : Prop := PolyTimeOn P.Domain (answer P)

/-- `P` reduces to `Q` in polynomial time on the admissible words of `P`. -/
def PolyReduces (P Q : Problem) : Prop := ∃ R, IsReduction P Q R ∧ PolyTimeOn P.Domain R

/-- A language of bit strings as a problem on words of zeros and ones. -/
def ofLanguage (A : Language) : Problem where
  Domain := {x | ∀ v ∈ x, v < 2}
  Yes x := x.map (fun v => decide (v = 1)) ∈ A
  param _ := 0

/-- `P` is **NP-hard**. -/
def NPHard (P : Problem) : Prop := ∀ A ∈ NP, PolyReduces (ofLanguage A) P

/-- On every admissible word, one program computes `F` within
`(bitSize x + 2) ^ f (κ x)` instructions, for a computable `f`. -/
def XPTimeOn (D : Set (List ℕ)) (κ : List ℕ → ℕ) (F : List ℕ → List ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (p : Program) (f : ℕ → ℕ), Computable f ∧ ∀ x ∈ D,
    FitsInWords ((bitSize x + 2) ^ f (κ x)) ((x.length :: x) ++ F x) ∧
      ∀ w : ℕ, (bitSize x + 2) ^ f (κ x) ≤ w →
        ∃ t ≤ (bitSize x + 2) ^ f (κ x), RunsTo w p (x.length :: x) (F x) t

/-- **XP**. -/
def XP : Set Problem := {P | IsParameterized P ∧ XPTimeOn P.Domain P.param (answer P)}

/-- The words of parameter at most `k`. -/
def slice (P : Problem) (k : ℕ) : Problem where
  Domain := {x | x ∈ P.Domain ∧ P.param x ≤ k}
  Yes := P.Yes
  param := P.param

/-- `P` is **para-NP-hard**. -/
def ParaNPHard (P : Problem) : Prop := ∃ k, NPHard (slice P k)

/-- `A` refines `B`. -/
structure Refines (A B : Problem) : Prop where
  domain : A.Domain ⊆ B.Domain
  yes : ∀ x ∈ A.Domain, (A.Yes x ↔ B.Yes x)
  param : ∀ x ∈ A.Domain, A.param x = B.param x

variable {A B : Problem}

axiom inP_of_refines : Refines A B → InP B → InP A
axiom fpt_of_refines : Refines A B → B ∈ FPT → A ∈ FPT
axiom xp_of_refines : Refines A B → B ∈ XP → A ∈ XP
axiom npHard_of_refines : Refines A B → NPHard A → NPHard B
axiom paraNPHard_of_refines : Refines A B → ParaNPHard A → ParaNPHard B
axiom hard_of_refines (𝒞 : Set Problem) : Refines A B → Hard 𝒞 A → Hard 𝒞 B

variable {K : Kernel} {F : Family K}

axiom refines_of_le_kernel (C : Coding F) (hF : F.Sound) {s t : Spec F} (h : s.le t)
    (κ : K.Inst → ℕ) :
    Refines (wordProblem C s (ofKernel F κ s)) (wordProblem C t (ofKernel F κ t))

axiom refines_of_le_field (C : Coding F) (hF : F.Sound) {s t : Spec F} (h : s.le t)
    (i : F.ModuleName) (κ : FieldParameter (F.module i)) (hκ : κ.Invariant) :
    Refines (wordProblem C s (ofField F i κ s)) (wordProblem C t (ofField F i κ t))

end Lax434175.ComplexityClasses

concepts.title: Bounds on the number of machines and jobs
concepts.description:
A count of a kernel assigns a natural number to every instance, such as its
number of machines or its number of jobs. The bound field of a count has the
values

- at most $k$, for every number $k$: the count is at most $k$, and at least
  a least number given with the count ($1$ for machines, $0$ for jobs);
- constant: no restriction on the instances; the value records that the
  count is regarded as a constant, as in the notation $n = k$;
- unlimited: the count is at least the number of jobs, as in the notation
  $P\infty$ for a machine for every job;
- at most one more than the jobs: the count is at most the number of jobs
  plus one, as in the notation $n \ge m - 1$ for the number $m$ of machines;
- any: no restriction.

At most $k$ is a special case of at most $l$ for $k \le l$, of constant and
of any; the other values are special cases of any.

In the three-field notation, $P2$ denotes two machines. Here it is read as at
most two machines and at least one, so that the problems with fewer machines
are special cases: an instance with one machine is an instance with at most
two. An instance without machines belongs to no problem with a bounded number
of machines.

**Theorem.** Over every kernel, for every count and every least number, the
bound field is sound.

import Lax434175.Modules

/-!
---
title: Bounds on the number of machines and jobs
type: theorem
---
A count of a kernel assigns a natural number to every instance, such as its
number of machines or its number of jobs. The bound field of a count has the
values

- at most $k$, for every number $k$: the count is at most $k$, and at least
  a least number given with the count ($1$ for machines, $0$ for jobs);
- constant: no restriction on the instances; the value records that the
  count is regarded as a constant, as in the notation $n = k$;
- unlimited: the count is at least the number of jobs, as in the notation
  $P\infty$ for a machine for every job;
- at most one more than the jobs: the count is at most the number of jobs
  plus one, as in the notation $n \ge m - 1$ for the number $m$ of machines;
- any: no restriction.

At most $k$ is a special case of at most $l$ for $k \le l$, of constant and
of any; the other values are special cases of any.

In the three-field notation, $P2$ denotes two machines. Here it is read as at
most two machines and at least one, so that the problems with fewer machines
are special cases: an instance with one machine is an instance with at most
two. An instance without machines belongs to no problem with a bounded number
of machines.

**Theorem.** Over every kernel, for every count and every least number, the
bound field is sound.
-/

namespace Lax434175.Counts
open Lax434175.Kernels Lax434175.Modules

inductive Bound
  | atMost (k : ℕ)
  | constant
  | unlimited
  | atMostJobsPlusOne
  | any

/-- The numbers admitted by a bound, given the number of jobs. -/
def Bound.holds : Bound → (jobs count : ℕ) → Prop
  | .atMost k, _, n => n ≤ k
  | .constant, _, _ => True
  | .unlimited, jobs, n => jobs ≤ n
  | .atMostJobsPlusOne, jobs, n => n ≤ jobs + 1
  | .any, _, _ => True

def Bound.le : Bound → Bound → Bool
  | _, .any => true
  | .atMost k, .atMost l => decide (k ≤ l)
  | .atMost _, .constant => true
  | .constant, .constant => true
  | .unlimited, .unlimited => true
  | .atMostJobsPlusOne, .atMostJobsPlusOne => true
  | _, _ => false

/-- The numbers admitted by a bound, given the number of jobs and the least
number that a bound `at most k` admits. -/
def Bound.admits (least : ℕ) (v : Bound) (jobs n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  v.holds jobs n ∧ ∀ k, v = .atMost k → least ≤ n

/-- The bound field of a count; a bound `at most k` admits the counts from
`least` to `k`. -/
def module (K : Kernel) (count : K.Inst → ℕ) (least : ℕ := 0) : Module K :=
  Module.ofRestriction Bound (fun v x => v.admits least (K.jobs x) (count x)) Bound.le

axiom sound (K : Kernel) (count : K.Inst → ℕ) {least : ℕ} : (module K count least).Sound

end Lax434175.Counts

statements.signature: sound : ∀ (K : Lax434175.Kernels.Kernel) (count : K.Inst → Nat) {least : Nat}, (Lax434175.Counts.module K count least).Sound

concepts.title: Deadlines
concepts.description:
The deadline field has three values. With the value "none" an instance
carries no deadlines. With the value "deadlines" it carries a deadline
$\bar d_j$ for every job $j$, which is a natural number or $\infty$, and every
job must complete by its deadline. With the value "common deadline" it
carries one deadline $\bar d$ for all jobs.

An instance without deadlines is read as an instance with the common
deadline $\infty$, and a common deadline as the deadline of every job.

**Theorem.** Over every kernel, the deadline field is sound.
concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib.Data.ENat.Basic
import Lax434175.Modules

/-!
---
title: Deadlines
type: theorem
---
The deadline field has three values. With the value "none" an instance
carries no deadlines. With the value "deadlines" it carries a deadline
$\bar d_j$ for every job $j$, which is a natural number or $\infty$, and every
job must complete by its deadline. With the value "common deadline" it
carries one deadline $\bar d$ for all jobs.

An instance without deadlines is read as an instance with the common
deadline $\infty$, and a common deadline as the deadline of every job.

**Theorem.** Over every kernel, the deadline field is sound.
-/

namespace Lax434175.Deadlines
open Lax434175.Kernels Lax434175.Modules

inductive Value
  | none
  | common
  | deadlines

/-- No data without deadlines; one deadline per job with them. -/
def Data (K : Kernel) : Value → K.Inst → Type
  | .none, _ => Unit
  | .common, _ => ℕ∞
  | .deadlines, x => Fin (K.jobs x) → ℕ∞

/-- The deadline of a job; `∞` when the field is absent. -/
def view {K : Kernel} {x : K.Inst} : (v : Value) → Data K v x → Fin (K.jobs x) → ℕ∞
  | .none, _ => fun _ => ⊤
  | .common, d => fun _ => d
  | .deadlines, d => d

def le : Value → Value → Bool
  | .deadlines, .none | .deadlines, .common | .common, .none => false
  | _, _ => true

def embed {K : Kernel} : {v w : Value} → le v w = true → (x : K.Inst) → Data K v x → Data K w x
  | _, .none, _, _, _ => ()
  | .none, .common, _, _, _ => (⊤ : ℕ∞)
  | .common, .common, _, _, d => d
  | v, .deadlines, _, _, d => view v d
  | .deadlines, .common, h, _, _ => absurd h Bool.false_ne_true

/-- A time is within a deadline. -/
def Within (c : NNRat) : ℕ∞ → Prop
  | none => True
  | some d => c ≤ (d : NNRat)

/-- The deadline field over a kernel. -/
def module (K : Kernel) : Module K where
  Value := Value
  Data := Data K
  admits _ _ _ := True
  constraint v x d σ := ∀ j, Within (K.completion x σ j) (view v d j)
  le := le
  embed := embed

axiom sound (K : Kernel) : (module K).Sound

end Lax434175.Deadlines

statements.signature: sound : ∀ (K : Lax434175.Kernels.Kernel), (Lax434175.Deadlines.module K).Sound

concepts.title: Maximum lateness against deadlines
concepts.description:
The maximum lateness is at most $D$ exactly if some schedule meets the
deadlines $\bar d_j = d_j + D$; a schedule that meets them has makespan at
most the largest of them. So the decision version of a problem minimizing the
maximum lateness without deadlines reduces to that of the problem with the
deadlines $d_j + D$ that minimizes the makespan, with the largest deadline as
threshold. If some $d_j + D$ is negative, or there are no jobs and $D$ is
negative, the threshold is $-1$.

A specification $s$ of the family with operations, or of the batching family,
reduces to $t$ through deadlines if $s$ minimizes the maximum lateness without
deadlines and the specification obtained by giving it deadlines and the
makespan as objective is field by field a special case of $t$. The relation is
decidable.

**Theorem.** In both families, a specification that reduces to another through
deadlines describes a problem whose decision version reduces to that of the
other.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax434175.OperationsFamily
import Lax434175.BatchFamily

/-!
---
title: Maximum lateness against deadlines
type: theorem
---
The maximum lateness is at most $D$ exactly if some schedule meets the
deadlines $\bar d_j = d_j + D$; a schedule that meets them has makespan at
most the largest of them. So the decision version of a problem minimizing the
maximum lateness without deadlines reduces to that of the problem with the
deadlines $d_j + D$ that minimizes the makespan, with the largest deadline as
threshold. If some $d_j + D$ is negative, or there are no jobs and $D$ is
negative, the threshold is $-1$.

A specification $s$ of the family with operations, or of the batching family,
reduces to $t$ through deadlines if $s$ minimizes the maximum lateness without
deadlines and the specification obtained by giving it deadlines and the
makespan as objective is field by field a special case of $t$. The relation is
decidable.

**Theorem.** In both families, a specification that reduces to another through
deadlines describes a problem whose decision version reduces to that of the
other.
-/

namespace Lax434175.DeadlineSteps
open Lax434175.Problems Lax434175.Assembly
open Lax434175

/-- The value without deadlines. -/
def noDeadlines : Deadlines.Value → Bool
  | .none => true
  | _ => false

/-- The specification with deadlines and the makespan as objective. -/
def opsWithDeadlines (s : Spec OperationsFamily.family) : Spec OperationsFamily.family where
  module
    | .deadlines => Deadlines.Value.deadlines
    | i => s.module i
  objective := .makespan

/-- `s` minimizes the maximum lateness without deadlines, and with deadlines and
the makespan it is field by field a special case of `t`. -/
def OpsReducesThroughDeadlines (s t : Spec OperationsFamily.family) : Prop :=
  Thresholds.objectiveOf s = .lmax ∧ noDeadlines (s.module .deadlines) = true ∧ (opsWithDeadlines s).le t

instance (s t : Spec OperationsFamily.family) : Decidable (OpsReducesThroughDeadlines s t) := by
  unfold OpsReducesThroughDeadlines
  infer_instance

/-- The batching specification with deadlines and the makespan as objective. -/
def batchWithDeadlines (s : Spec BatchFamily.family) : Spec BatchFamily.family where
  module
    | .field .deadlines => Deadlines.Value.deadlines
    | i => s.module i
  objective := .makespan

def BatchReducesThroughDeadlines (s t : Spec BatchFamily.family) : Prop :=
  Thresholds.objectiveOf s = .lmax ∧ noDeadlines (s.module (.field .deadlines)) = true ∧
    (batchWithDeadlines s).le t

instance (s t : Spec BatchFamily.family) : Decidable (BatchReducesThroughDeadlines s t) := by
  unfold BatchReducesThroughDeadlines
  infer_instance

axiom ops_reducible {s t : Spec OperationsFamily.family} :
    OpsReducesThroughDeadlines s t →
      Reducible (problem OperationsFamily.family s) (problem OperationsFamily.family t)

axiom batch_reducible {s t : Spec BatchFamily.family} :
    BatchReducesThroughDeadlines s t →
      Reducible (problem BatchFamily.family s) (problem BatchFamily.family t)

end Lax434175.DeadlineSteps

  Lax434175.DeadlineSteps.BatchReducesThroughDeadlines s t →

      (Lax434175.Assembly.problem Lax434175.BatchFamily.family t)

concepts.title: Results between parameters of one problem
concepts.description:
A parameter $\kappa'$ of a problem is *dominated* by a parameter $\kappa$ if
$\kappa'(x, D) \le g(\kappa(x, D))$ for a function $g$ and every instance $x$ and
threshold $D$. Then the identity on words is an fpt-reduction from the problem
with $\kappa$ to the problem with $\kappa'$ when $g$ is computable, and the
words with $\kappa \le k$ are among those with $\kappa' \le g(0) + \dots + g(k)$.

**Theorem.** If $\kappa'$ is dominated by $\kappa$, then para-NP-hardness and
W[t]-hardness for $\kappa$ hold for $\kappa'$, and membership in XP and
fixed-parameter tractability for $\kappa'$ hold for $\kappa$ ($g$ computable for
the last two).

Two dominations of the zoo's parameters: a summand is dominated by a sum, and
on the operations family the number $\#p$ of distinct processing times is at
most $p_{\max} + 1$ (the values lie in $\{0, \dots, p_{\max}\}$).

**Theorem.** These dominations hold.

namespace Lax434175.Domination
open Lax434175 Lax434175.Problems Lax434175.Results Lax434175.ResultParameters
open Lax496464.WH_A2_FptReductions

variable {P : Problem}

/-- `κ'` is bounded by `g` of `κ` on every instance and threshold. -/
def Dominated (κ' κ : TParameter P) (g : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop := ∀ x D, κ' x D ≤ g (κ x D)

axiom paraNPHard_of_dominated {R : PReading P} {κ κ' : TParameter P} {g : ℕ → ℕ}
    (h : Dominated κ' κ g) : ParaNPHard R κ → ParaNPHard R κ'

axiom wHard_of_dominated {R : PReading P} {κ κ' : TParameter P} {g : ℕ → ℕ} (t : ℕ)
    (hg : Computable g) (h : Dominated κ' κ g) : WHard R t κ → WHard R t κ'

axiom inPFixed_of_dominated {R : PReading P} {κ κ' : TParameter P} {g : ℕ → ℕ}
    (h : Dominated κ' κ g) : InPFixed R κ' → InPFixed R κ

axiom isFPT_of_dominated {R : PReading P} {κ κ' : TParameter P} {g : ℕ → ℕ}
    (hg : Computable g) (h : Dominated κ' κ g) (hp : IsParameterized (parameterized R κ)) :
    IsFPT R κ' → IsFPT R κ

axiom left_tplus (κ κ' : TParameter P) : Dominated κ (tplus κ κ') id

axiom right_tplus (κ κ' : TParameter P) : Dominated κ' (tplus κ κ') id

axiom ops_numP_pmax (s : Assembly.Spec OperationsFamily.family) :
    Dominated (lift (Ops.numP s)) (lift (Ops.pmax s)) (· + 1)

concepts.title: Relations of the Scheduling Zoo that need an encoding
concepts.description:
Eight relations of The Scheduling Zoo do not compare two specifications field
by field, and are not threshold steps: the more special problem has to be
encoded in the more general one by changing the instance.

**Just in time inside on time.** On a single machine, a job with processing
time $p_j$ and due date $d_j$ completes exactly at its due date if and only
if it is on time and starts no earlier than $d_j - p_j$. Hence
$1 \mid\mid \sum Z_j$ is a special case of $1 \mid r_j \mid \sum U_j$ with
the release dates $r_j = d_j - p_j$, and likewise with weights.

**A single machine inside a two-machine flow shop.** A job of the single
machine becomes a job with an operation of length $0$ on the first machine
followed by its operation on the second machine. Hence the decision version
of $1 \mid\mid \sum Z_j$ reduces to that of $F2 \mid\mid \sum Z_j$, and
likewise with weights.

**Flow shops and parallel machines inside the two-stage flexible flow
shop.** A two-machine flow shop is a two-stage flexible flow shop with one
machine in the second stage, and a problem on identical parallel machines is
one in which every first operation has length $0$. Hence the decision
versions of $F2 \mid\mid \sum Z_j$ and of $P \mid\mid \sum Z_j$ reduce to
that of $FF(1,m) \mid\mid \sum Z_j$, and likewise with weights.

The relations across machine models are stated for decision versions,
because a problem on parallel machines has instances without machines and
hence without schedules, which a shop problem cannot represent by an
instance but only by an unreachable threshold.

Each reduction across machine models is stated with its effect on the
numbers of jobs and machines: the number of jobs is unchanged; the flow shop
has two machines, and the flexible flow shop of a problem on $m$ parallel
machines has $m + 1$, that of a flow shop two.

**Theorem.** These eight relations hold, with these numbers of jobs and
machines.

import Lax434175.ParallelProblems

/-!

title: Relations of the Scheduling Zoo that need an encoding

---

$1 \mid\mid \sum Z_j$ is a special case of $1 \mid r_j \mid \sum U_j$ with
the release dates $r_j = d_j - p_j$, and likewise with weights.

**A single machine inside a two-machine flow shop.** A job of the single
machine becomes a job with an operation of length $0$ on the first machine
followed by its operation on the second machine. Hence the decision version
of $1 \mid\mid \sum Z_j$ reduces to that of $F2 \mid\mid \sum Z_j$, and
likewise with weights.

**Flow shops and parallel machines inside the two-stage flexible flow
shop.** A two-machine flow shop is a two-stage flexible flow shop with one
machine in the second stage, and a problem on identical parallel machines is
one in which every first operation has length $0$. Hence the decision
versions of $F2 \mid\mid \sum Z_j$ and of $P \mid\mid \sum Z_j$ reduce to
that of $FF(1,m) \mid\mid \sum Z_j$, and likewise with weights.

The relations across machine models are stated for decision versions,
because a problem on parallel machines has instances without machines and
hence without schedules, which a shop problem cannot represent by an
instance but only by an unreachable threshold.

Each reduction across machine models is stated with its effect on the
numbers of jobs and machines: the number of jobs is unchanged; the flow shop
has two machines, and the flexible flow shop of a problem on $m$ parallel
machines has $m + 1$, that of a flow shop two.

**Theorem.** These eight relations hold, with these numbers of jobs and
machines.
-/

namespace Lax434175.Encodings
open Lax434175 Lax434175.Problems Lax434175.Assembly Lax434175.Parameters

/-- `1 || γ` -/
def single (objective : Objectives.Value) : Spec ParallelProblems.nonpreemptive :=
  ParallelProblems.spec _ (environment := .identical) (machineCount := .atMost 1)
    (objective := objective)

/-- `1 | r_j | γ` -/
def singleRelease (objective : Objectives.Value) : Spec ParallelProblems.nonpreemptive :=
  ParallelProblems.spec _ (environment := .identical) (machineCount := .atMost 1)
    (release := .releaseDates) (objective := objective)

/-- `P || γ` -/
def identical (objective : Objectives.Value) : Spec ParallelProblems.nonpreemptive :=
  ParallelProblems.spec _ (environment := .identical) (objective := objective)

/-- `F2 || γ` -/
def flow2 (objective : Objectives.Value) : Spec ShopProblems.family :=
  ShopProblems.spec (shopType := .flow) (machineSets := .byPosition) (machineCount := .atMost 2)
    (objective := objective)

/-- `FF(1,m) || γ` -/
def flexibleFlow (objective : Objectives.Value) : Spec ShopProblems.family :=
  ShopProblems.spec (shopType := .flexibleFlow) (machineSets := .stages) (objective := objective)

/-- The numbers of jobs and machines of an instance on parallel machines. -/
def parallelSize {s : Spec ParallelProblems.nonpreemptive}
    (x : Inst ParallelProblems.nonpreemptive s) : ℕ × ℕ :=
  (x.base.jobs, x.base.machines)

/-- The numbers of jobs and machines of a shop instance. -/
def shopSize {s : Spec ShopProblems.family} (x : Inst ShopProblems.family s) : ℕ × ℕ :=
  (x.base.jobs, x.base.machines)

axiom justInTime_onTime :

axiom weightedJustInTime_onTime :

concepts.title: Machine sets encoded by long processing times
concepts.description:
On unrelated machines every processing time is finite, and the problems on
unrelated machines have no machine sets. A machine on which job $j$ may not run is instead encoded by a
processing time too long for every schedule within the threshold. Four
relations of the Scheduling Zoo rest on this encoding; each maps an instance
with machine sets $M_j$ and threshold $D$ to an instance on unrelated machines
with the same jobs, machines and times $p_{ij}$ for $i \in M_j$, and a long
time for $i \notin M_j$.

- $P \mid M_j \mid C_{\max}$ to $R \mid\mid C_{\max}$ and
  $Q \mid M_j \mid \sum C_j$ to $R \mid\mid \sum C_j$: the time $D + 1$. A job
  on a machine outside its set completes after $D$, so a schedule within the
  threshold uses only the machines of the sets, and it is a schedule of the
  instance with machine sets of the same cost. A job without a machine in its
  set makes both instances infeasible within the threshold.
- $P \mid M_j \mid \sum w_jC_j$ to $R \mid\mid \sum w_jC_j$: the time
  $D + 1$ again. A job of positive weight on a machine outside its set costs
  more than $D$; a job of weight $0$ costs nothing anywhere and is moved to
  the end of a machine of its set. An instance with a job whose set is empty
  is mapped to a threshold that no schedule meets.
- $P \mid M_j \mid \sum w_jZ_j$ to $R \mid\mid \sum w_jZ_j$: the time
  $d_j + 1$, so a job outside its set is never just in time; such jobs are
  moved to the end of a machine of their set, which makes no just-in-time job
  late. An instance with a job whose set is empty is mapped to a threshold
  that no schedule meets.

**Theorem.** The decision version of each of the four problems with machine
sets reduces to that of the problem on unrelated machines, with the same
numbers of jobs and machines.

The reduction is computed on the standard words: a program reads the word of an
instance with machine sets and its threshold and writes the word of the
unrelated instance and its threshold, in polynomial time and with numbers at
most one more than those it reads. So hardness goes up along the four
relations.

**Theorem.** Along each of the four relations, NP-hardness and strong
NP-hardness on the standard reading go from the problem with machine sets to the
problem on unrelated machines, and so does W[t]-hardness for the number of
machines.

import Lax434175.ZooParallel
import Lax434175.Parameters
import Lax434175.StandardReading

/-!
---
title: Machine sets encoded by long processing times
type: theorem
---
On unrelated machines every processing time is finite, and the problems on
unrelated machines have no machine sets. A machine on which job $j$ may not run is instead encoded by a
processing time too long for every schedule within the threshold. Four
relations of the Scheduling Zoo rest on this encoding; each maps an instance
with machine sets $M_j$ and threshold $D$ to an instance on unrelated machines
with the same jobs, machines and times $p_{ij}$ for $i \in M_j$, and a long
time for $i \notin M_j$.

- $P \mid M_j \mid C_{\max}$ to $R \mid\mid C_{\max}$ and
  $Q \mid M_j \mid \sum C_j$ to $R \mid\mid \sum C_j$: the time $D + 1$. A job
  on a machine outside its set completes after $D$, so a schedule within the
  threshold uses only the machines of the sets, and it is a schedule of the
  instance with machine sets of the same cost. A job without a machine in its
  set makes both instances infeasible within the threshold.
- $P \mid M_j \mid \sum w_jC_j$ to $R \mid\mid \sum w_jC_j$: the time
  $D + 1$ again. A job of positive weight on a machine outside its set costs
  more than $D$; a job of weight $0$ costs nothing anywhere and is moved to
  the end of a machine of its set. An instance with a job whose set is empty
  is mapped to a threshold that no schedule meets.
- $P \mid M_j \mid \sum w_jZ_j$ to $R \mid\mid \sum w_jZ_j$: the time
  $d_j + 1$, so a job outside its set is never just in time; such jobs are
  moved to the end of a machine of their set, which makes no just-in-time job
  late. An instance with a job whose set is empty is mapped to a threshold
  that no schedule meets.

**Theorem.** The decision version of each of the four problems with machine
sets reduces to that of the problem on unrelated machines, with the same
numbers of jobs and machines.

The reduction is computed on the standard words: a program reads the word of an
instance with machine sets and its threshold and writes the word of the
unrelated instance and its threshold, in polynomial time and with numbers at
most one more than those it reads. So hardness goes up along the four
relations.

**Theorem.** Along each of the four relations, NP-hardness and strong

-/

concepts.title: Fine-grained hypotheses and reductions on short words
concepts.description:
The hypotheses of fine-grained complexity, stated in the style of the
exponential time hypothesis (`Results.ETH`): on the word RAM of lax-808846, with
short words, $\ell \ge c \log_2(|u| + M + 2)$ for the input $u$ with largest
number $M$, so that a program cannot pack many numbers into one word. Each is
about an explicit problem on words. Problems with numbers have them polynomial in
the input size, as the literature states these conjectures.

- **SETH**: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $k$ such that no program decides
  the satisfiability of formulas with clauses of at most $k$ literals over $n$
  variables within $c\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}(|w|+1)^c$ instructions.
- **Orthogonal vectors**: given $n$ and $d$ and two lists of $n$ vectors in
  $\{0,1\}^d$, is some vector of the first list orthogonal to some of the
  second? For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $a$ such that with $d \le a \log_2 n$
  no program decides it within $c\,n^{2-\varepsilon}$.
- **3SUM**: given $n$ integers of absolute value at most $n^3$, do three of them
  (at different positions) sum to $0$? No program decides it within
  $c\,n^{2-\varepsilon}$, for any $\varepsilon > 0$.
- **APSP**: given a complete directed graph on $n$ vertices with integer arc
  lengths of absolute value at most $n^3$ and no negative cycle, write the
  matrix of shortest distances; no program does so within $c\,n^{3-\varepsilon}$.
- **Min-plus convolution**: given two lists of $n$ integers of absolute value
  at most $n^3$, write $c_k = \min_{i+j=k}(a_i + b_j)$; no program does so within
  $c\,n^{2-\varepsilon}$.
- **$k$-Clique**: with $\omega$ the infimum of the exponents $e$ such that a
  program multiplies $n \times n$ matrices of integers of absolute value at most
  $n$ within $c\,n^e$ instructions, for every $k \ge 3$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ no
  program decides whether a graph on $n$ vertices has $k$ pairwise adjacent
  vertices within $c\,n^{(\omega/3-\varepsilon)k}$.

Integers are written as sign and absolute value; vectors, lists and matrices
entry by entry after their sizes; a graph as $n$ and its adjacency matrix.

A **fine-grained reduction** from a problem on words to another is one program
that maps the words of the first to words of the second, keeps the answer, runs
